10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Observed data have been collected using a variety of methods over time and space, but these methodological differences are expected to have little bearing on the overall conclusions for this indicator. The concordance of trends among multiple data sets collected using different program designs provides some assurance that the trends depicted actually represent changes in atmospheric conditions, rather than an artifact of sampling design.

The observed and projected time series cover the same global spatial extent. Due to global mixing and long residence times in the atmosphere, measurements from specific locations are widely understood to adequately represent concentrations worldwide, though the graph for methane (the gas with the shortest atmospheric lifetime of the three gases profiled) does show that relatively small variations can be apparent across different locations.

11. Data Limitations

The three gases profiled here are not the only greenhouse gases or radiatively important substances that influence climate change. However, these three gases are particularly important, as shown by their relative contributions to warming in the Climate Forcing indicator. The technical documentation for the Atmospheric Concentrations of Greenhouse Gases indicator also describes some limitations inherent in dating ice core samples.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. However, direct measurements of atmospheric concentrations, which cover approximately the last 50 years, are of a known and high quality. Generally, standard errors and accuracy measurements are computed for the data. For ice core measurements, uncertainties result from the actual gas measurements, as well as the dating of each sample. Uncertainties associated with the measurements are believed to be relatively small, although diffusion of gases from the samples might also add to the measurement uncertainty. Dating accuracy for the ice cores is believed to be within ± 20 years, depending on the method used and the time period of the sample. This level of uncertainty is insignificant, however, considering that some ice cores characterize atmospheric conditions for time frames of hundreds of thousands of years. The original scientific publications noted above provide more detailed information on the estimated uncertainty within the individual data sets. Visit the Carbon Dioxide Information Analysis Center (CDIAC) archive for more information on the accuracy of both direct and ice core measurements.

Overall, the increase in greenhouse gas concentration in the past century is far greater than the estimated uncertainty of the underlying measurement methodologies. It is impossible that the concentration trends depicted in this set of figures are artifacts of uncertainty.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

13. Sources of Variability

Atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases can vary with both time and space. Considerations include seasonal cycles (for example, see the full Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record shown in the Keeling Curve) and regional variations. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Focusing on long-lived greenhouse gases that are globally mixed.
  • Using annual averages to reduce some of the day-to-day “noise” and seasonal signals inherent in sub-annual instrumental measurements.

The additional 800,000 years of historical data in the Atmospheric Concentrations of Greenhouse Gases indicator provide extraordinary temporal context for interpreting recent and projected future concentrations.
